front_question: How is a triangle formed from intersecting lines, and how are triangles classified by side lengths?
back_answer: Three lines intersecting pairwise at three distinct points form a triangle. Classification: 1. Equilateral (all sides equal). 2. Isosceles (two sides equal). 3. Scalene (all sides unequal).

front_question: State the Triangle Inequality Theorem and its practical testing shortcut.
back_answer: Triangle Inequality Theorem: A triangle exists if and only if the sum of any two side lengths is strictly greater than the third side (a + b > c, b + c > a, c + a > b). Shortcut test: The sum of the two smallest sides must be strictly greater than the longest side.

front_question: What happens during ruler and compass triangle construction if side lengths fail the triangle inequality (e.g. 3, 3, 7)?
back_answer: When drawing compass arcs of radii 3 cm from endpoints of base 7 cm, the arcs fail to intersect because 3 + 3 = 6 < 7, visually proving no triangle can be formed.

front_question: Why is an equilateral triangle always constructible for any positive side length s > 0?
back_answer: For an equilateral triangle, all three sides equal s. The triangle inequality requires s + s > s => 2s > s. Since s > 0, 2s > s is universally true for all positive numbers s.
